Renan’s judgments about Arab philosophy became widely known.
He may have been the first person in nineteenth-century Europe to popularize the claim that it was wrong to call the Greek philosophy transmitted into Arabic “Arab philosophy.”

According to him, what was called Arab philosophy was really no more than a body of writings produced as a reaction against Arabism in the regions of the Islamic Empire furthest from the Arabian Peninsula—places such as Samarkand, Bukhara, Córdoba, and Marrakesh.
These philosophical works were written in Arabic only because Arabic had become the language of science and religion throughout the Islamic world. In Renan’s view, that was the whole story.
Renan even rejects the claim that the Arabs preferred Aristotle to other Greek philosophers.
He argues that there was no genuine preference, because preference requires choice, and the Arabs had made no deliberate choice after reflection.
“The Arabs simply adopted Greek culture in the form in which it reached them…”
In the note that introduced the second edition of his book Averroes and Averroism, Renan repeated the same position:
“The Arabs did nothing more than adopt the whole Greek encyclopedia as the world encountered it around the seventh and eighth centuries.”
What concerns us here is not the judgment itself about Arab philosophy.
What matters at this point is the basis on which that judgment rests.
Renan makes that basis clear in the introduction to the first edition of his book, where he says openly:

“It is not from the Semitic race that we should expect lessons in philosophy. One of the strange ironies of history is that this race, which was able to give its religious creations such extraordinary power, produced almost nothing original in philosophy. Among the Semites, philosophy was little more than something borrowed from outside, without great fertility of its own—essentially an imitation of Greek philosophy…”
The danger of this racial “theory” lies in the fact that it became a wider intellectual current.
Renan was only one of its most prominent theorists.
After him, racial ideas became one of the foundations used in a number of Orientalist studies and formed part of imperialist ideology.
Among the Orientalists who continued this line of thought was Léon Gauthier, formerly a professor of history at the University of Algiers and a “well-known enthusiast for colonial rule.”
Gauthier added new claims to Renan’s distinction between Semites and Aryans.
He argued that the “Semitic mind” could see things only as separate and unconnected, while the “Aryan mind” was able to bring things together, connect them, and form them into a coherent whole.
Starting from this arbitrary racial distinction, he presents Islam as a strongly Semitic religion standing in opposition to Greek philosophy, which he presents as strongly Aryan.
He then places the Islamic philosophers between these two supposedly opposing worlds.
According to him, they tried with great skill to bridge the gap, but even the tools they used came from Greek philosophy itself.

Their work, on this account, was simply “Aryan” thinking trying to create a gradual connection between two opposing forms of thought: Islamic thought, supposedly based on separation, and Greek thought, supposedly based on connection.
Gauthier uses the same colonial racial framework when judging the Moroccan people.
Among the white peoples of the Mediterranean basin, he describes Moroccans as the culturally different group that had “remained far behind.”
Other Western Orientalists followed the same general current.
One was the German Orientalist Christian Lassen (1876), known for dividing peoples into Semitic and Aryan groups and for his hostility toward the “Semitic race.”
Another was Émile Bréhier, professor of the history of philosophy at the Sorbonne, who also supported the distinction between Semites and Aryans.
Starting from this idea, Bréhier speaks about the philosophers of Islam in much the same way as Renan.

He argues that although they wrote their philosophical works in Arabic, most were not Semitic in origin but Aryan. This, according to him, explains why they looked for their philosophical subjects in Greek thought and also in the Mazdakite ideas of Persia, which in turn were mixed with Indian ideas.
The Orientalist Stanla, known for his lectures at the Egyptian University on the history of philosophy, followed a similar approach.
He too begins with racial assumptions when explaining the history of philosophy and of Islam.
In discussing the meaning of Islam, for example, he says:

“…This absolute submission in everything, which is often an original characteristic of the Semites, is the defining principle of Islam and distinguishes it among peoples. Perhaps a vague awareness of a similar connection between this opposition and the religious instinct characteristic of the Arab people was what led Muḥammad to proclaim that he was the revealer of the true and original religion of Abraham and the Seal of the Prophets…”
Modern science has made the falsehood of dividing humanity according to “race” and racial characteristics so clear that there is no need for us to discuss the question at length here.
Specialized scientific works provide detailed evidence against it.
A readily accessible Arabic source on the subject is the recently published book The Racial Problem in Islam.
It summarizes the findings of modern anthropologists, sociologists, and psychologists—even bourgeois scholars—who have rejected the foundations of racial theories.
But we need to be careful here.
The fact that bourgeois scholars have been forced by modern scientific evidence to abandon racial theories does not mean that they have abandoned the social uses those theories served.
Those uses continue to appear both in the field of class struggle and in the struggle between imperialism and peoples seeking national liberation.
Second: the view that philosophy has its true center in the West, not the East.
This may be another form of the racial classification of the world’s peoples, but it has its own distinctive basis.
Its intellectual roots are different from those of explicit “race theory,” even though its class and political roots are much the same.
The theory of a Western center of philosophy begins from a real feature of human cultural history: the unity of human culture appears in forms that can look contradictory.
Because of this, it is very easy to treat the distinctive features of each national culture as absolute, and then to treat the differences between national cultures as absolute as well.
From there, a complete “theory” can be built.
This is exactly what happened among a number of European philosophers and thinkers in the nineteenth century.
Hegel (1770–1831), for example, passed the following judgment on Eastern philosophy:

“What we call Eastern philosophy consists essentially, and to a very great extent, of the religious form of ideas and beliefs found among Eastern peoples—ideas and beliefs that at first sight we take to be philosophy.”
We need to remember that Hegel’s judgment had another basis as well: his view of the relationship between religion and philosophy.
Hegel believed that religion appeared historically before philosophy.
Through religion, peoples expressed their ideas about the essence of the universe, the nature of the world, Absolute Spirit, and the relationship of human beings to all of these.
Because religion came before philosophy historically, Hegel regarded it as the first form through which Absolute Spirit came to know itself.
Even so, Hegel did not believe that the history of philosophy should include the history of religions.
Religion and philosophy may share certain features, but he believed there were also important differences between them.
Most importantly, philosophy approaches its subject through thinking consciousness, while religion approaches it through an immediate relationship to a higher reason.
Hegel says that the form through which the content of “science” properly enters the field of philosophy is thought—the universal and absolute form of thinking.
Religion, by contrast, presents the same content through artistic form, through direct outward contemplation, and then through representation and feeling.
For Hegel, philosophy therefore stands above religion because it understands “Absolute Spirit” in a form more appropriate to spirit itself.
As for philosophical elements that may be hidden inside religion, Hegel does not consider them part of philosophy proper.
As he explains, his concern is philosophy itself, not philosophical elements in the abstract and not ideas that remain hidden inside myths.
This is why Hegel argued that Eastern philosophy should be removed from the history of philosophy.
Eastern philosophy may contain profound ideas, he says, but those ideas remain hidden within other forms.
He continued to insist on this position.

“Eastern thought must be removed from the history of philosophy. I will nevertheless make a few remarks about it. In the past I remained completely silent about it. Only recently have we been given the possibility of judging it.”
We do need to take this background into account when examining Hegel’s judgment on Eastern philosophy.
But there is another factor behind that judgment as well.
It may seem that Hegel simply lacked enough knowledge of the original sources of Eastern philosophy.
If that was indeed the case, however, it does not excuse him.

By the first quarter of the nineteenth century, when Hegel was delivering his lectures on the history of philosophy, enough information about Eastern cultures and their philosophical traditions was already available in Europe to allow a more accurate judgment and a sounder understanding of how philosophy had developed in the East.
The problem, then, was not simply a shortage of sources or ignorance of them.
It lay in Hegel’s philosophical method and in the way he approached the subject.

His strict definition of philosophy was also influenced by positions common among the bourgeois philosophers of Western Europe in his time, especially their views about the supposed difference between the ways people think in Eastern and Western societies.
For many decades, bourgeois European writing was dominated by the claim that Eastern and Western people had fundamentally different ways of thinking.
According to this view, Eastern thought was irrational, synthetic, and intuitive or sensory, while Western thought was rational and analytical.
Once that distinction had been accepted, it naturally followed that the intellectual products of each side would also be treated as fundamentally different from those of the other.
Philosophy was inevitably included in this distinction.
The American social thinker F. S. C. Northrop followed this line in his book The Meeting of East and West. The German writer W. Haas did the same, as did many others.

The problem with Eurocentrism in philosophy is, first, that its supporters turned the relationship between Eastern and Western ways of thinking into an opposition. Second, they ignored the basic unity of human thought and treated the real differences within it as absolute differences, as we will explain.

But was this theory of philosophical centrality based only on problems of knowledge—on the complex and contradictory nature of knowledge itself—or did it also rest on an ideological foundation? Problems of knowledge alone cannot fully explain this trend. The theory of centrality also had, above all, class roots. In other words, it had an ideological basis.

As capitalism developed into imperialism, it needed an intellectual and ideological justification for its domination of Asia and Africa even more than it needed a political one. In those conditions, the bourgeois claim that Eastern culture was generally irrational, sensory, and religious served a particular political purpose. It naturally gave the “rational” European a justification for ruling the “irrational” Asian.

Today, bourgeois philosophers such as Northrop still hold to the theory of Eurocentrism. But its supporters now have to find new arguments in its defence. In its classical form, the theory can no longer justify itself under new conditions simply by appealing to Eastern “irrationality.”

Earlier changes had already forced some adjustments to the theory. New standards appeared for deciding where the centre of philosophy lay. America could not simply be treated as part of Europe, yet there was a desire to include it within the philosophical centre, and America could not plausibly form a separate centre of its own. So the idea of “Western-centrism” replaced “Eurocentrism,” allowing the supposed centre to include both Europe and America.

But with the broad rise of national liberation movements in Asia and Africa, another trend naturally appeared. It answered “Western-centrism” with an opposing form of centrality: “Eastern-centrism,” or “Asian-African centrism.”

This opposing trend also has both intellectual and social roots. Its intellectual roots resemble those that produced Western-centrism. Its social roots lie in the rise of the peoples of Asia and Africa, regions that had been major centres in the early development of human civilization.

But we should note that the people who represent this Asian-African form of centrism are not, of course, representatives of the working class. They represent the bourgeoisie, the petty bourgeoisie, the feudal class, and large landowners.

Asian-African centrism appears mainly in two forms. The first is an exaggerated account of the role played by Eastern culture and philosophy in the development of European philosophy—even in the development of Marxism. The second is the tendency to treat the religious and mystical elements within the national cultures of Asia and Africa as absolute.

We have already mentioned one example: the report presented by the Pakistani scholar Sharif to the Twelfth World Congress of Philosophy in 1951. Another can be found in the ideas of the poet and philosopher Léopold Senghor, who is currently president of Senegal.

In explaining his idea of Négritude, Senghor describes it as the complete set of cultural, economic, social, and political values that distinguish the Black world, or the African Black world. He says that these values were created mainly by a sensory form of reason—a form of reason that enters into things and expresses itself through emotion, through self-surrender, through the merging of subject and object, and through myths, which he regards as archetypes of the collective spirit.

To all this he adds a primal rhythm in harmony with the rhythm of the universe. In other words, there is a feeling of connection with nature, the symbolism of myth-making, and rhythm. These, Senghor says, are “the essential elements of Black philosophy, whose traces you can find in every work and every activity of the Black person.”
Having quoted this, we are faced with a question. Given Senghor’s definition of Black philosophy, how does he judge rationalist philosophies that differ from it?

Senghor says that “the civilization of analytical reason proves capable of creating a world of machines deprived of human warmth.” Or, as he puts it elsewhere, Black philosophy is a human philosophy, while European philosophies are essentially anti-human. He then places Marxism at the very summit of European rationalism.

One Soviet philosopher comments that the danger of such ideas appears when they are raised to the level of a general law. If they are made absolute in the way Senghor’s words suggest, then that danger is real: one racist position may arise to fight another racist position.

That makes it difficult to accept Jean-Paul Sartre’s interpretation when he comments on Senghor’s own account of the African tendency, given in 1948. Sartre acknowledges that “Négritude is racist,” but describes it as “anti-racist.” In his view, it “represents a moment of negation and a synthesis (Synthèse) produced in reaction to white superiority and privilege. It is the antithesis (Antithèse) in a dialectical sequence that leads to a final synthesis, which in turn gives rise to a universal humanity free of racism.”

But racism is racism, and it can never be anything else. It is poetic fantasy to imagine that an equation of this kind will somehow produce a humanity free of racism. Senghor’s own statements about Négritude, and his absolute rejection of European philosophies, support this conclusion.

In fact, the appearance of a theory of Asian-African centrism under present world conditions—the conditions of national liberation movements and of labour movements in capitalist countries—does nothing to help unite the worldwide revolutionary movement.
